newsitem.title: INDIA: Investment to spur Indian recovery - Chidambaram.
newsitem.headline: Investment to spur Indian recovery - Chidambaram.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said on Saturday that the economy, hamstrung by lacklustre industrial growth and sluggish exports, would accelerate in the year to March 1998 once investment picked up.
"Once investment picks up, you will see the turnaround coming," Chidambaram told reporters.
He said that while public investment had been stepped up in the current fiscal year, private investment was not forthcoming.
Chidambaram urged companies to borrow money from banks, raise funds from capital markets and step up investment.

"For last two years, beginning December 1995, they (private sector) have put their investment proposals on the shelf. I am saying them to take those proposals out, dust them, and start investing," Chidambaram said.
Exports -- critical to India's growth -- fell 10.1 percent in April to $2.52 billion from $2.81 billion in the same month last year.
Industrial output grew by 7.5 percent in the first 10 months of 1996/97 compared with an 11.7 percent rise in the corresponding period in the previous year.
But the rate of growth slowed substantially in the second half of 1996/97, and in February it was just 2.4 percent higher than in the same month in 1996.
Chidambaram said high interest rates, tight liquidity, low consumer demand and a slackening in investment had hampered growth last year.
But since the Reserve Bank of India eased credit conditions in April, the liquidity had improved, he said.
Leading banks cut their prime lending rates by one to 1.5 percentage points to 14.0-14.5 percent after the central bank unveiled its six-monthly monetary policy on April 16.
"Banks are flush with funds," Chidambaram said.
He hoped better liquidity conditions and lower interest rates would encourage private firms to borrow from banks and step up investment.
An anticipated bumper grains harvest in 1996/97 (July-June) would also boost consumer spending in 1997/98.
Chidambaram said he did not believe that industrial growth would be weaker in 1997/98 than the previous fiscal year.
"In fact, I think industrial growth will sharply pick up thanks to the bountiful (grains) harvest of 192 million tonnes."

Chidambaram said a quick decision on oil prices was crucial to plug a mounting oil pool deficit. The oil pool account deficit represents money the government owes domestic oil firms to compensate them for selling some petroleum products at below global prices.
Asked how much longer the government could wait before deciding whether to raise the prices of some petroleum products, Chidambaram said: "Not very long. A solution has to be found."
The ruling United Front would decide whether to raise prices of domestic petroleum products at the coalition's next meeting, scheduled to be held on June 27, he said.
"We will reach a decision collectively next time," the finance minister said.

At its last meeting on June 16, the 15-party United Front postponed a decision on whether to raise prices to plug the government's mounting debt to state oil companies, estimated at 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) at the end of March.
Left-wing parties in Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's alliance have strongly opposed any price increase and submitted an alternative plan to raising oil prices.
Chidambaram said he had an "alternative to the alternative plan", but did not elaborate.
